aflcio_description: The proposal - Motion by Rep. Albert (D-Okla.) to keep liberalized House rules adopted by 89th Congress. Background - The House Rules Committee's ability to stall legislation indefinitely was curbed by the 89th Congress. On opening day of the 90th Congress Albert made an unsuccessful parliamentary move to assure the liberalized House rules would continue in effect. The vote - On motion to save liberalized rules. Rejected, 196-225, January 10, 1967. Yea - right. Nay - wrong.

The proposal - Amendment by Rep. Davis (R-Wis.) to cut $10 million from rent supplements program. Background - The 89th Congress enacted a rent supplement program to help poor families live in decent housing. Funding the program has been a constant battle although it is the first housing subsidy program ever endorsed by all segments of the real estate industry. Despite this, House conservatives voted to cut the rent supplements plan. The vote - On the amendment. Approved, 233-171, May 17, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - Motion by Rep. Michel (R-Ill.) to strip model cities program of $225 million in project funds. Background - Enacted in 1966, the model cities program was designed to renovate slums and blighted neighborhoods. It provides federal financial and technical aid to cities. It was intended to develop means for a comprehensive attack on social economic and physical problems that beset the slums and the poor who live in them. The vote - On motion to cripple model cities program. Rejected, 193-213, May 17, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - Amendment by Rep. Green (D-Ore.) that would in effect undermine key parts of the aid to education program under the guise of "states rights." Background - one of the great and hopeful breakthroughs of the 89th Congress was passage of the first major federal aid program to elementary and secondary schools. The law has helped school children in 90 percent of the nation's school districts, but its main achievement has been to aid children from low-income families. This "states rights" amendment transferred control of funds for fresh-idea programs to state boards of education, most of which work with outmoded distribution formulas weighted in favor of rural systems and against the deep-need core city school systems. The vote - On the amendment. Approved, 230-185, May 24, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - Agriculture Committee amendment to destroy the food stamp program. Background - The food stamp program helps millions of poor persons eat better at minimum cost. They pay, for example, $3 for government stamps worth three or four times that amount when exchanged for food. It is one of the most humane of all federal programs. The committee amendment called for passing 20 percent of the program's cost to the states. Its effect would have been that most of the 41 states now participating would have withdrawn, according to their own governors and welfare directors. The vote - On the amendment. Rejected, 173-191, June 8, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - Motion by Rep. Gurney (R-Fla.) to kill the Teachers Corps. Background - The Teachers Corps was established to give deprived children an extra boost in education. It sends specially-trained teachers into the slums. Since its inception, it has been a target of reactionaries despite its modest cost. The vote - On the motion to kill the Teachers Corps. Rejected, 146-257, June 27, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - A motion by Rep. Friedel (D-Md.) to accept Senate-passed compulsory arbitration legislation, forcing striking rail shopcraft workers back to work. Background - The first nationwide rail strike in more than 20 years began July 15, 1967. It ended two days later when Congress forced workers back to their jobs to await a settlement by a presidential panel. Compulsory arbitration was vigorously opposed by the labor movement as a dangerous federal intervention in labor-management affairs and an infringement of basic collective bargaining rights of both labor and management. The vote - On accepting Senate-passed legislation to force strikers back to work. Approved, 244-148, July 17, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - A proposal to bring to the floor for consideration the Rat Extermination Act. Background - Rats are disease-spreaders. They bite 14,000 Americans each year, mostly children and mostly in city slums. They cause $1 billion loss damage in food and goods annually. The proposal was greeted with jests and frivolity by some representatives. The vote - On the proposal to consider the President's rat control program. Rejected, 176-207, July 20, 1967. Yea - right. Nay - wrong.

The proposal - Amendment by Rep. Giaimo (D-Conn.) to the public work appropriations bill, to cut the $1.6 million in planning funds for Dickey-Lincoln power project in Maine. Background - The Dickey-Lincoln power project has been the center of a public vs. private power battle. The project was designed to bring abundant power at low cost to a depressed region where power rates are among the highest in the country. The vote - On the proposal to knock out planning funds for Dickey Lincoln. Approved, 233-169, July 25, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - A motion by Rep. Gross (R-Iowa) to reduce salary increases for postal workers and other federal civilian employes. Background - Federal salaries do not match salaries for equivalent jobs in private industry. An effort was made to bring postal workers and other federal civilian employes in line with private industry salaries by a multi-step salary increase over three years. The proposal by Gross would have killed all but the first-step increase. The vote - On the motion to delete all but the first step of salary increases. Rejected, 199-211, Oct. 11, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - An amendment by Rep. Whitten (D-Miss.) to force an $8.5 billion cut in the administration's budget for fiscal 1968. Background - Seeking to embarrass the President, conservatives tried a series of maneuvers to slash and to stall appropriations bills throughout the first session of the 90th Congress. Their main target, apart from harassment, was to force starvation of new Great Society programs through cuts in appropriations for labor, education, health, housing, welfare and the war on poverty. The vote - On the amendment. Approved, 238-164, Oct. 18, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The proposal - Motion by Rep. Ayres (R-Ohio) to slash $460 million from the Office of Economic Opportunity (command post for the war on poverty) authorization. Background - Conservatives waged war on the war on poverty throughout the first session of the 90th Congress. Their objective was to dismantle the OEO and "spin off" poverty program to other federal agencies where the programs would lose impact and effectiveness. While dismantling efforts were defeated, the deep slash in funds from a proposed $2.06 billion to $1.6 billion would severely limit OEO operations, and would curtail or kill useful anti-poverty programs in many areas. The vote - On the motion. Approved, 221-190, Nov. 15, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

One of the big accomplishments of the 90th Congress was extension of federal meat inspection standards to the billions of pounds of meat which had been exempt because it wasn't sold across state lines. The Senate made major improvements in the original, very weak House bill. The conservative coalition voted down a motion to accept the Senate amendments which required states to match federal inspection standards. A public outcry finally brought approval of a good bill, but this attempt to strengthen the meat inspection law was beaten, 166-207, on Nov. 29, 1967. For - right; Against - wrong.

Final passage of the 1968 civil rights legislation would have been endangered if the House had not agreed to accept Senate amendments and instead insisted on sending the bill to a conference committee. The legislation outlawed housing discrimination, protected civil rights workers, and made it a federal crime to enter a state with the intent to take part in a riot. A conference would have opened the door to a new Senate filibuster and endangered the legislation. Church, labor and civil rights organizations pressed for a House vote on acceptance of the Senate-passed bill. The resolution which cleared the way for final passage was adopted, 229-195, on Apr. 10, 1968. For - right; Against - wrong.

Conservatives insisted on - and got - a deep budget cut in return for going along with a tax increase the President said was essential to the nation's economy. Earlier, Administration supporters sought to reduce the amount of the budget slash - a compromise which would have permitted high priority programs to continue while reducing funds for less urgent matters. This compromise was rejected by the House, 137-259, on May 29, 1968. For - right; Against - wrong.

A Republican motion to slash $100 million from anti-poverty funds would have deprived thousands of children of participation in the Head Start program and forced the closing of 13 Job Corps centers - slamming the door shut on training opportunities for young men and women. Adoption of the motion would have served notice that Congress and the nation was preparing to abandon the war on poverty as "too costly" for the world's richest nation. The cutback was rejected, 181-220, on June 26, 1968. For - wrong; Against - right.

Decent homes for all Americans would go a long way toward meeting the nation's most pressing problems. An important step was taken in this year's housing legislation. It provides for building 1.7 million new or rehabilitated housing units in the next three years for low and moderate income families. It includes interest subsidies to help low income families buy homes and incentives for apartment-builders to provide low-rent units. Other sections of the legislation expand rent supplement and model cities programs. The housing bill was passed, 295-114, on July 10, 1968. For - right; Against - wrong.

One of the great breakthroughs of recent years was legislation providing federal aid to education. It has aided more than 90 percent of all American school districts, with particular emphasis on poverty areas. One of its strengths had been the ability of school administrators to plan several years in advance for the use of expected federal funds. However, Rep. Green (D-Ore.) proposed an amendment limiting extension of the school aid plan to two years instead of five and giving states control over part of the federal funds. Her amendment was approved 235-184, Apr. 23, 1969. For - wrong. Against - right.

Some large farm owners get vast subsidy payments from the government. Sen. Eastland (D-Miss.), for example, receives approximately $150,000 a year in subsidies. Rep. Conte (R-Mass.) proposed limiting subsidy payments to $20,000. This was approved 225-142, May 27, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

Over opposition of labor and other tax reform forces, the House extended the surtax on income tax one year without including meaningful tax reform. However, the margin was so close before the vote that it brought firm pledges from House Ways & Means Chairman Mills and Pres. Nixon to consider tax reform immediately. This paved the way for reforms and the $750 personal exemption in the final tax measure signed into law. The measure passed June 30, 1969 by a vote of 210-205. For - wrong. Against - right.

The Administration budget called for totally inadequate funding of federal aid to education - less than half the amount Congress had authorized to be spent. The House Appropriations Committee recommended an additional $121 million for education aid. But the gap between that amount and the need would still have been too wide in the opinion of labor and education groups. The AFL-CIO helped rally support for an amendment by Rep. Joelson (D-N.J.) to add an additional $894.5 million for education programs. It was approved 294-119, July 31, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

Nixon's HEW appropriations requests, to provide adequate funds for needed health and education programs, the President vetoed the measure, charging the additional funding was inflationary. A proposal to override the veto won a 226-191 majority, Jan. 28, 1970, but fell short of the two-thirds majority necessary to override. For - right. Against - wrong.

The 1965 Voting Rights Act has helped add more than a million voters to the registration rolls in seven southern states and has been the most successful human rights legislation in recent years. An Administration move to weaken it succeeded narrowly in the House in December 1969. But the Senate restored the act to its original form - concentrating in seven states - and added the voting franchise for 18-year-olds and standardized residency requirements for voting for president. When it came before the House again, Rep. Matsunaga (D-Hawaii) moved to accept the AFL-CIO-supported Senate version. His motion carried June 17, 1970, 224-183. For - right. Against - wrong.

Construction and modernization of urgently needed health facilities were threatened by Pres. Nixon's veto of a bill extending the Hill-Burton program of federal grants. This was another instance of a presidential veto aimed at funding of an important social welfare program. The veto came only a year after the President himself had warned that the nation is in a health crisis and "unless action is taken . . . we will have a breakdown in our medical care system affecting millions." The vote to override the veto far exceeded the necessary two-thirds majority, June 25, 1970, 279-98. For - right. Against - wrong.

Farm workers, whose employment is mainly seasonal and who suffer long stretches of joblessness, are not covered by unemployment insurance. It was rejected July 23, 1970, 170-219. For - right. Against - wrong.

The AFL-CIO and civil rights groups strongly supported legislation giving the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission the enforcement power necessary to stop illegal job discrimination. Business groups and the Administration, however, backed a weak substitute that denied enforcement power to EEOC and limited action to court suits. The House voted, 202-197, against effective enforcement and for the substitute bill on Sept. 16, 1971. For - wrong. Against - right.

Although federal employes were scheduled to receive a comparability salary increase on Jan. 1, 1972, the President, as part of his "wage freeze," attempted to defer this increase until July 1, 1972. The House by a 174-207 vote on Oct. 4, 1971, failed to pass a resolution that would have overturned the President's postponement of catch-up pay for federal employes. For - right. Against - wrong.

During House consideration of campaign reform legislation, Rep. Hansen (R-Ida.) offered an amendment clarifying court rulings on union political activities. The amendment made it clear that organized labor has the right to spend funds from dues income to communicate with members and conduct non-partisan registration and get-out-the-vote drives aimed at members and their families. Passage of the Hansen amendment blocked an announced effort by Rep. Crane (R-Ill.) to offer an amendment severely limiting labor's political rights. On Nov. 30, 1971, the House approved the Hansen amendment by a vote of 233-147. For - right. Against - wrong.

The need for decent day care for the children of America's millions of working women was recognized by both the House and Senate. As reported by a conference committee, the new bill provided voluntary comprehensive day care services with a fee schedule based on ability-to-pay. Despite all-out Administration opposition, the House approved the badly needed new day care program, by a 211-187 vote on Dec. 7, 1971. The President then vetoed the measure and the Senate failed to override. For - right. Against - wrong.

Legislation extending the President's wage-price control authority cleared the House Banking Committee with a provision permitting back pay for most wage increases that were due during the Phase 1 freeze. The bill was crippled on the House floor when an amendment sponsored by Rep. Stephens (D-Ga.) was approved. The Stephens amendment limited back pay to those cases where an employer had already raised prices to cover the increase, and thereby ruled out most retroactive pay boosts. The damage was later repaired in House-Senate conference. On Dec. 10, 1971, the House adopted the Stephens amendment by a 209-151 vote. For - wrong. Against - right.

Late in the session, Congress approved a 13-week extension of unemployment compensation benefits for an estimated 538,000 workers who had exhausted basic and extended unemployment compensation. This temporary program, starting in February, provides aid to workers who are the victims of long-term unemployment in states with the highest jobless rates. The emergency program was included as part of a conference report approved by the House on Dec. 15, 1971, by a 194-149 vote. For - right. Against - wrong.

Ignoring the fact that the West Coast Longshoreman's Union (ILWU) and management had reached agreement in their seven-month long contract dispute, the House bowed to strong White House pressure and passed legislation providing for a ban on further strike activities and compulsory arbitration of all unresolved contract differences. The AFL-CIO strongly opposed this legislation as an unwarranted intrusion into the collective bargaining process. The key vote on this proposal was on a motion to adopt a procedural rule which would allow for a vote on the compulsory arbitration bill. Despite labor's opposition the rule was adopted by a 203-170 roll call vote on Feb. 9. For - wrong. Against - right.

Despite strong labor opposition to this Administration-backed substitute bill, introduced by Rep. John Erlenborn (R-Ill.), the House adopted the measure by a 217-191 recorded teller vote on May 11. For - wrong. Against - right.

This amendment, strongly opposed by organized labor, would have excluded more than 25 per cent of the workers and 86 per cent of the job sites presently covered by the law. Particularly hard hit would have been construction and farm workers. Although the House on June 15 approved the Findley amendment by a 213-154 recorded teller-vote, the final conference report on the bill weakened the effect of this amendment. For - wrong. Against - right.

Despite threats of a presidential veto, the Hathaway amendment, supported by organized labor and education groups, was approved, 212-163, on June 15. For - right. Against - wrong.

Striking workers and their families have always been entitled to food stamps as long as they complied with the stringent eligibility requirements under the program. During House action on a farm bill, Rep. William Dickinson (R-Ala.) offered an amendment to deny food stamps to strikers and their families. The Dickinson amendment was approved by the House on July 19 by a 213-203 vote although later dropped from the bill before final passage. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: tally 273-144 -> 274-143 per Voteview roll 328
aflcio_description: Because "The Emergency Medical Services Act of 1973" included a provision prohibiting the Administration from phasing out eight existing Public Health Service hospitals, President Nixon vetoed this labor-supported legislation. On Sept. 12, the House fell five votes short of the two-thirds needed to override the President's action. The vote to override was 273-144. Later in the session, the ban against closing Public Health Service hospitals without the consent of Congress was written into a high-priority Defense Dept. authorization bill which the President signed into law. For Overriding - Right. Against - Wrong.

Despite skyrocketing consumer prices and an ever increasing number of families living in poverty, President Nixon on Sept. 6 vetoed as "inflationary" the labor-supported minimum wage bill. The House vote on Sept. 19 to override the veto was 259-164, falling 23 votes short of the two-thirds majority required to overcome a presidential veto. For Overriding - Right. Against - Wrong.

During House debate on legislation reorganizing seven bankrupt railroads, Rep. Dan Kuykendall (R-Tenn.) offered an anti-labor amendment to limit the period of compensation for railroad workers who lost their jobs or took pay cuts because of the reorganization. His amendment was rejected by a 187-198 vote on Nov. 8. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Administration opposition to a number of Senate amendments to the Alaskan pipeline bill, particularly a consumer protection provision, moved the conservative coalition in the House to oppose adoption of a House-Senate conference report on the pipeline legislation. Rep. William Steiger (R-Wis.) attempted to send the legislation back to conference with instructions to delete the consumer provisions. Labor strongly opposed this maneuver and the House rejected the Steiger motion by a 162-213 vote on Nov. 12. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Although strongly opposing final passage of the trade bill, the AFL-CIO supported the adoption of an amendment to the bill sponsored by Rep. Charles Vanik (D-Ohio) prohibiting government-backed credits or loan guarantees to the Soviet Union until such time as it eased its restrictive emigration policies. By an overwhelming 319-80 vote, the House on Dec. 11 approved the Vanik amendment. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The AFL-CIO has long urged enactment of the Burke-Hartke trade bill in order to curb the loss of American jobs resulting from unregulated imports, the export of U.S. capital and technology and the runaway of American industry to low-wage areas of the world. However, the House Ways & Means Committee reported out an Administration-backed bill giving the President blank-check authority to deal with trade problems on a selective basis. Despite strong labor opposition, the House on Dec. 11 approved the bill by a 272-140 vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Despite efforts by the Chamber of Commerce, National Association of Manufacturers and other anti-consumer lobbies, the House rejected an amendment by Rep. Clarence Brown (R-Ohio) designed to cripple labor-supported legislation establishing a federal consumer protection agency. The amendment, beaten by a 176-223 margin on Apr. 3 would have limited the agency's powers to seek judicial redress on behalf of consumers who had been injured or defrauded. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

During debate on the 1974 supplemental appropriations bill, Rep. David Obey (D-Wis.) offered a labor-backed amendment providing an additional $150 million for job-creating public service employment programs. Without this additional funding, this federal jobs program would have been cut back at a time when national unemployment exceeded 5 percent and was increasing. The key vote came on Apr. 10 as the House approved the Obey amendment by a 236-168 vote. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Fearing an increase in low-income and black voter participation, Republicans and southern Democrats combined forces to sidetrack labor-supported legislation making it easier for the public to register through a national postcard voter registration system. The defeat of the bill came when the House by a 197-204 vote on May 8 rejected a parliamentary motion to consider the rule under which the bill would be debated. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: date 1974-05-16 -> 1974-05-15 per Voteview roll 690
aflcio_description: Congress completed action in 1974 on legislation establishing an independent legal services corporation to provide free legal help to poor people who could not otherwise afford such assistance. Rep. John Erlenborn (R-Ohio) tried to gut the legislation by having a House-Senate compromise recommitted to conference with instructions that would have resulted in severely restricting the legal services available to the poor. The recommittal motion was rejected on May 16 by a 183-190 vote. For Recommittal - Wrong. Against - Right.

In an effort to combat rising fuel prices and windfall oil industry profits, Rep. Harley Staggers (D.-W.Va.) sponsored emergency energy legislation providing the President with powers to cope with the energy crisis and including price rollbacks on domestically produced crude oil and price ceilings on imported oil. The measure also established an unemployment compensation fund for workers losing their jobs as a result of the energy crisis. However, in a key vote on May 21 the House failed by a 191-207 vote to muster the two-thirds vote necessary to pass this bill under an expedited parliamentary procedure. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: tally 186-201 -> 186-200 per Voteview roll 730
aflcio_description: For ten years the planned Dickey-Lincoln power plant - designed to supply New England states with low cost electrical power - has failed to get off the drawing boards because of opposition by private utility interests. In 1974, preconstruction planning funds for this project were included in the fiscal 1975 Public Works appropriations bill. During debate on the bill, the House rejected by a 186-201 vote June 6 an effort to strike Dickey-Lincoln funds from the bill. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

The lack of a coordinated and effective national land use policy and decision-making process has led to serious environmental problems including pollution, rural decline, urban sprawl and resource depletion. Organized labor strongly supported Senate passed legislation providing federal coordination, minimum standards, grants and technical assistance to the states in the formulation of their land use policies. Conservative Republicans and southern Democrats backed by land speculators and real estate interests, raised the spectre of "big government" to kill the bill before it reached the House floor. The key vote came June 11 when the House by a 204-211 vote rejected the parliamentary motion to approve the rule under which the bill would be debated. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Striking workers and their families have always been entitled to food stamps as long as they complied with the stringent eligibility requirements under the program. During House action on the Agriculture Appropriations bill, Rep. William Dickinson (R-Ala.) offered an amendment to deny food stamps to strikers and their families. The Dickinson amendment was rejected by the House on June 21 by a 147-169 vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

In the second session of the 93rd Congress efforts were again made to seriously weaken the Occupational Safety & Health Act. In debate on the Labor-HEW appropriations bill, Rep. Paul Findley (R-Ill.) introduced an amendment to exempt firms employing 25 or fewer employes from coverage under the act. This amendment excluded more than 30 percent of the workers and 90 percent of the job sites presently covered by law. Despite strong labor opposition to this anti-worker amendment, the House on June 27 approved the Findley proposal by a 201-194 recorded teller-vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Since 1947 when the Taft-Hartley Act excluded non-profit hospital workers from coverage under the National Labor Relations Act, these workers, numbering an estimated 1.3 million in 1973, have been denied the basic trade union rights taken for granted by millions of other workers. In 1974, Congress remedied this situation by passing legislation bringing these workers under NLRA protection. The key vote in the House came on July 11 when by a 205-193 vote the House approved the conference report giving non-profit hospital workers collective bargaining rights. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: tally 164-213 -> 164-243 per Voteview roll 876
aflcio_description: During House action on the federal election campaign reform bill, Rep. William Dickinson (R-Ala.) attempted to include a provision that would have severely crippled COPE-type political campaign activities. If approved, Rep. Dickinson's recommittal motion would have required each union voluntary campaign fund to include the name of every contributor as well as individual specified candidates to whom the contribution would be given. In a key vote, however, the House on Aug. 8 rejected the Dickinson amendment by a 164-213 vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

A combination of runaway inflation and budget cuts in education by the Nixon and Ford Administrations has played a major role in the current financial crisis facing the nation's schools. To alleviate this situation, the House, in debate on the fiscal 1976 Education Appropriations bill, approved 259-143 on Apr. 16 an amendment by Representatives Roybal (D-Calif.), Obey (D-Wis.), and Stokes (D-Ohio) increasing education spending by $487 million. President Ford's later veto of this appropriations bill was overridden. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Despite declining farm income and skyrocketing production costs which have financially squeezed small farmers, President Ford vetoed a one-year emergency farm bill that would have improved income guarantees to farmers while protecting consumers. The legislation had the strong backing of labor, consumer and various farm groups. On May 13, the House by a 245-182 vote fell 40 votes short of the two-thirds margin needed for override. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Amid threats of still another presidential veto, the House on May 20 passed 312-86 a public works authorization bill allocating $5 billion in federal aid to states and local communities for public works construction programs. Needed public works programs are high on the AFL-CIO agenda because they create useful jobs. First priority for spending under the legislation was given to those areas where unemployment exceeded the national rate. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: tally 134-279 -> 133-279 per Voteview roll 183, the bail-out amendment the card describes; roll 182 of the same day matches the printed yea at 134-269 but is the WIGGINS substitute where the card names Butler, and the roster grid picks 183 at 100% against 182's 92%
aflcio_description: The 1965 landmark Civil Rights Act curbed the use of discriminatory voting practices and has resulted in significant increases in minority voting participation. Labor-supported legislation extending the act for 10 years and broadening its protections was passed by Congress and signed into law in 1975. Prior to House passage of the bill, Rep. Butler (R-Va.) offered a crippling amendment allowing states to be exempted from coverage if they met certain minimal "escape" provisions. The proposal was strongly opposed by labor, civil rights and other groups, and the House rejected it 134-279 on June 3. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

With the recession deepening and national unemployment at 9.2 percent - the highest since 1941 - President Ford in late May vetoed labor-backed emergency employment legislation appropriating $5.3 billion to create over 1 million jobs for the unemployed. The AFL-CIO General Board had recommended enactment of such legislation to stimulate economic recovery and relieve high unemployment. The House effort to override this veto on June 4 was blocked by a coalition of conservative Democrats and Republicans and the 277-145 override vote fell 5 votes short of the necessary two-thirds margin. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Labor-backed environmental legislation providing minimum federal standards for state development of mandatory strip mining control laws became another veto victim of President Ford in 1975. The legislation was in response to serious environmental devastation caused by surface mining companies in their strip mining operations. In an effort to override the veto on June 10, the House failed to muster the two-thirds vote needed as the 278-143 vote was three votes short. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: date 1975-06-04 -> 1975-06-25 per Voteview roll 259: the card repeats record 1's date for the housing veto override; 268-157 occurs once in the whole 94th House
aflcio_description: Legislation to stimulate the depressed housing industry - another program strongly backed by the AFL-CIO General Board - similarly fell victim to another Ford veto. The vetoed bill, by providing some $1.35 billion in housing subsidy assistance for both new construction and rehabilitation of more than 500,000 housing units over the next year, would have created an estimated 800,000 jobs in construction and related industries. The legislation also included a program of low-interest mortgage assistance loans to help jobless workers meet these payments. Once again the House effort to overcome Ford's veto was blocked by the conservative coalition as the 268-157 override vote on June 4 fell 16 votes short of the two-thirds margin needed. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

During debate on the Labor-HEW Appropriations bill, Rep. Findley (R-Ill.) renewed his yearly efforts to cripple the Occupational Safety & Health Act. His amendment would have prohibited the Occupational Safety & Health Administration from penalizing first violations of job safety regulations on any work site with fewer than 26 workers. His proviso would have effectively denied job safety protection to more than 30 percent of the workers and 90 percent of the work sites presently covered by the law. The proposal was strongly opposed by the AFL-CIO, and the House on June 25 rejected it 186-231. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: tally 230-178 -> 230-177 per Voteview roll 326
aflcio_description: The House on July 25 passed 230-178, legislation giving construction workers situs picketing rights. Sought by organized labor since 1951 when a Supreme Court decision had interpreted such action to be an illegal secondary boycott, the bill gave building tradesmen the same rights that industrial workers have to picket a job site in order to publicize a dispute with their employers. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Despite record high profits of the energy industry over the past few years directly contributing to the nation's inflationary problems, the oil lobby continued its efforts in 1975 to seek decontrol of oil prices. The major effort came during House consideration of an omnibus energy conservation bill. The House rejected outright decontrol and instead approved a compromise proposal by Representatives Staggers (D-W.Va.) and Eckhardt (D-Tex.) retaining price controls on oil from existing wells, rolling back the inflated price of "new" oil and establishing a three-tier system of oil pricing. The labor-backed amendment was approved by a 218-207 vote on July 30. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Prior to passage of the labor-backed comprehensive energy bill, the Ford Administration, bowing to oil industry opposition to the bill, threatened a veto of the measure. In a last-ditch effort to kill it, Rep. Brown (R-Ohio) attempted to have the bill recommitted to eliminate the price control provisions. The House rejected the Brown recommittal motion 171-232 on Sept. 23. For Recommittal - Wrong. Against Recommittal - Right.

The 1939 Political Activity Act, commonly known as the Hatch Act, now prohibits some 2.8 million federal and postal employes from participating in partisan political activities. Reform legislation designed to correct this inequity while also strengthening existing restrictions against political coercion of federal workers was passed by the House in late 1975. During debate, the House on Oct. 21 rejected 147-260 an amendment by Rep. Fisher (D-Va.) that would have maintained nearly all the prohibitions against federal worker participation in the political process. The legislation is now before the Senate. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Amid continuing threats of a presidential veto, the House on Oct. 23 approved 261-129 labor-endorsed railroad legislation. The bill authorized $240 million for the employment of jobless railroad workers and others in the rehabilitation and repair of dilapidated railroad track and roadbeds. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Congress passed and the President signed into law legislation to restrict the practice of "redlining" certain urban areas by mortgage lenders. The redlining practice arbitrarily denies mortgage loans for housing and has been a major cause of inner-city decline. The House, in passing a comprehensive banking bill, included a provision requiring lenders in metropolitan areas to disclose over a four-year period the amount of mortgage money being made available in urban neighborhoods. The provision would thus discourage redlining and encourage credit allocation for inner city housing. During debate on the bill Rep. Brown (R-Mich.) attempted to gut this anti-discrimination feature by limiting it to only certain metropolitan areas. The House, however, rejected this attempt 165-167 on Oct. 31. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

In an effort to scuttle labor-backed legislation establishing an Agency for Consumer Advocacy, anti-consumer forces led by Rep. Fuqua (D-Fla.) sought to place labor-management relations within the new agency's jurisdiction. The amendment, strongly backed by the Chamber of Commerce, National Association of Manufacturers and other anti-consumer groups, was an effort to kill the legislation. The House on Nov. 6 rejected the amendment 175-233. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

During debate on the second budget resolution setting fiscal 1976 spending and revenue levels, the House on Nov. 12 approved 213-203 a labor-backed amendment offered by Rep. O'Neill increasing spending for programs including jobs and education. The amendment bumped funding by some $8.5 billion in budget authority and $1.1 billion in outlays over the Budget Committee recommendations. Of the total budget authority in the "package" amendment, 16 percent was for jobs and education. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

During House debate on a supplemental appropriations bill, Rep. Findley (R-Ill.) attempted to severely cripple the food stamp program. Findley's amendment would have effectively prohibited benefits to many needy people including the working poor, the elderly and the families of both unemployed and striking workers. The House, on November 13, rejected this crippling amendment 159-230. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

In action on the first major tax reform bill since 1969, the House rejected a labor-backed reform amendment further closing an important real estate tax loophole. Introduced by Rep. Mikva (D-Ill.), the proposal would have prevented real estate investors from offsetting actual profits from one property with artificial "paper losses" from another. The House rejected the amendment 192-226 on Dec. 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

A second tax reform amendment to reduce from five to three years the tax loophole allowing firms to defer export profits through the Domestic International Sales Corp. (DISC) programs was also defeated. Introduced by Rep. Karth (D-Minn.), this reform was rejected by 199-223 on Dec. 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Prior to passage, Rep. Schneebeli (R-Pa.) attempted to send the tax bill back to committee with instructions to add an Administration-backed federal spending ceiling for 1976. The ceiling was designed to force an indiscriminate federal spending cutback in exchange for President Ford's approval of the tax bill. The House rejected the move 202-220 on Dec. 4. For Recommittal - Wrong. Against Recommittal Right.

Although the real estate and DISC tax reform amendments were blocked, the House approved other major reform amendments strongly backed by the AFL-CIO. These amendments deleted from the bill a "give-away" provision allowing wealthy individuals to use current capital losses to recover past taxes, tightened the minimum tax on persons whose income would otherwise escape taxation and retained a withholding tax on earnings of foreign investors in U.S. firms. The bill also continued through 1976 tax reductions approved by Congress earlier in the year. The AFL-CIO thus supported final passage of the combination tax reform-tax cut bill which the House approved 257-168 on Dec. 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Essential to the national goal of energy independence is the continued development of nuclear power as an alternative energy source. The 1957 Price-Anderson Act, a mandatory multi-million dollar program of private and federal liability insurance, protects the public against loss in the event of an accident at a nuclear power plant site. This law has spurred the development of nuclear power from the experimental energy stage to where it now is a significant source of energy for consumers. Late in 1975, labor-endorsed legislation to extend this law for 10 years and increase the limits of liability was approved by Congress and signed into law. On Dec. 8 the House approved 329-61 extension of this important supplemental energy program. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Overcoming continuous opposition by anti-labor interests, the House on Dec. 11 approved 229-189 the conference report on the situs picketing bill. The conference-reported bill included earlier House-passed legislation sought by President Ford to promote stability in construction industry collective bargaining. Later, however, President Ford, reneging on earlier promises to sign the legislation and ignoring the past support of situs picketing by every President since Truman, buckled to right-wing and big business pressures and vetoed the labor bill. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The House rejected President Ford's veto of a $36 billion appropriations measure for the Departments of Labor and Health, Education & Welfare. The bill significantly increased funds for labor-backed manpower, health, education and job safety programs. The House voted 310-113 on Jan. 27 to override the President's action. The Senate also overrode this veto. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

A last minute effort by labor and consumer groups blocked almost certain passage of a proposal to deregulate the price of natural gas sold in interstate commerce. Long sought by the nation's energy interests and solidly backed by the Ford Administration, deregulation would have initially cost American consumers an estimated $5.4 billion yearly, increasing to over $17 billion annually in five to seven years. A compromise amendment by Rep. Smith (D-Iowa) which allowed partial price deregulation for only small gas producers but more importantly extended controls to previously unregulated intrastate gas was approved by a 205-201 vote Feb. 5. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The nation's federal aid to education program allocates funds to areas "impacted" by federal installations to help defray state and local educational costs of children whose families are employed by these installations. In recent years such "impact" aid was extended to locales having low-rent public housing to help pay the educational cost of children residing in these areas. Long-time antagonists of this program tried to block appropriations for it. During debate on legislation revising educational funding for 1976, Rep. Michel (R-Ill.) offered an amendment to eliminate the $98 million allocated for this educational aid. His amendment was rejected 134-267 on Feb. 10. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

With well over 7 million Americans unemployed, the House approved a two-year expansion of the labor-backed public service jobs program (CETA). The bill would effectively double the number of jobs available to 600,000. Despite increasing unemployment, the Administration sought only an extension of the program at existing levels. A substitute to this effect by Rep. Quie (R-Minn.) was rejected 175-226 Feb. 10. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Showing his continuing indifference to the plight of unemployed Americans, President Ford vetoed a $6.1 billion public works jobs bill. This was the third major employment bill approved by the 94th Congress to be erased by a presidential veto. The measure would have created an estimated 600,000 jobs primarily in the construction of much needed public facilities such as schools and libraries and water, sewer and pollution control projects. The House on Feb. 19 successfully overrode the veto by a 319-98 vote. However, the Senate later failed in this effort. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The AFL-CIO has urged termination of U.S. contributions to the United Nations Development Program (UNDP). This UN agency, which is charged with promoting economic growth and stability in under-developed nations, has squandered millions in funding and mismanaged projects which have never been completed. Meanwhile, eastern bloc countries and oil-rich Arab states have received funds far in excess of their contributions to the UNDP. During House debate on foreign aid appropriations for 1977, Rep. Edwards (R-Ala.) introduced an amendment to delete $85.5 million allocated to the UNDP. The House rejected his proposal 179-208 on Mar. 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

During House debate on legislation reconstructing the Federal Election Commission, conservatives offered a series of amendments to gag labor's political voice. The most serious of these was a proposal by Rep. Wiggins (R-Calif) designed to discourage union political activities by overloading local unions with cumbersome reporting requirements. The Wiggins amendment would have required that all the costs of communicating with members on any election matter would have to be reported. The House rejected the amendment 175-220 on Apr. 1. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

During House debate on a 1977 defense authorization bill, numerous attempts were made to block or delay development of various weapons systems. One such amendment offered by Rep. Seiberling (D-Ohio) would have deferred the expenditure of $960 million for the development of the B-1 strategic bomber until after Feb. 1977. The House rejected the amendment 177-210 on Apr. 8. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Another Ford veto blocked legislation giving nearly 2.8 million federal and postal employees the same rights now enjoyed by other Americans to participate in partisan political activities. President Ford based his veto on the erroneous assertion that the bill weakened existing protections against political coercion and intimidation of federal workers when in fact it significantly improved these safeguards. On Apr. 29 the House by a 243-160 margin failed by 25 votes to obtain the two-thirds vote needed to override the veto. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

A priority on labor's legislative agenda, this legislation would provide a mechanism to better coordinate national economic planning and direct it toward the primary economic goal of full employment. Designed to reduce national adult unemployment to a 3 percent rate within four years, the bill sets up a variety of federally-assisted jobs programs to be implemented if other methods of reducing unemployment fail. Start-up planning and administrative funds for the Humphrey-Hawkins bill were provided in the first Congressional Budget Resolution. An effort by Rep. Sarasin (R-Conn.) to strip these funds from the bill was rejected 177-206 on Apr. 29. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: bill HR9308 -> HR9803 per Voteview roll 782's own description and per Senate roll 776 on the same veto; Voteview's bill_number field transposes two digits
aflcio_description: President Ford vetoed a stopgap funding bill to help state child care centers comply with federal health and staffing requirements. Financially unable to meet these standards, many of these facilities would be closed down because federal funds would be cut off. Denial of these child care services would force many low-income working mothers back to welfare in order to care for their children. The House on May 4 easily overrode the veto by a 301-101 vote. However, on the following day the Senate sustained the veto. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The AFL-CIO strongly supports federal efforts to develop alternate sources of energy to meet the nation's long-term needs. Nuclear energy is one of these potential sources of power. During debate on legislation providing funds for the Energy Research & Development Administration for 1977, opponents of nuclear energy development again tried to block the continuing construction of the Clinch River breeder reactor demonstration project. An amendment by Rep. Coughlin (R-Pa.) placing severe financing restrictions on the project so as to delay its development was defeated 173-209 on May 20. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

To prevent jurisdictions utilizing federal revenue-sharing funds from evading the program's minimal Davis-Bacon Act fair wage requirements and thus pay wages lower than those prevailing in the area, the AFL-CIO sought to expand the wage coverage provisions in the revenue-sharing program. Under existing law only projects using 25 percent or more federal funds have to pay the prevailing rate. An amendment by Rep. O'Hara (D-Mich.) to require Davis-Bacon rates whenever any revenue sharing funds are used was defeated 174-218 on June 10. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The Administration's assault on programs to help the nation's needy continued in 1976. Singled out for special attack was the food stamp program, whose rolls have swelled as a result of soaring unemployment. Regressive Administration guidelines designed to slash millions of working poor and low-income families from the food stamp rolls were blocked by court action, but House conservatives tried to effect these changes through legislative action. During debate on the 1977 agricultural appropriations bill, Rep. Rousselot (R-Calif.) tried to slash over $794 million from the food stamp program. The House rejected his proposal by a 184-222 vote on June 16. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: tally 231-161 -> 231-160 per Voteview roll 944
aflcio_description: On June 24, during debate on a Labor-HEW appropriations bill, the House approved 231-161 an amendment by Rep. Findley (R-Ill.) seriously weakening the 1970 Occupational Safety & Health Act. By excluding firms employing 10 or fewer workers from coverage under the job safety law, this amendment would arbitrarily deny protection to 83 percent of all workplaces and 20 percent of all workers presently covered. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

During debate on the 1977 Labor-HEW appropriations bill on June 24, the House approved 183-181 an amendment by Rep. Mitchell (D-Md.) increasing funds for the Summer Youth Employment program. This program was created to combat the high rate of unemployment among young workers - more than double that of other age groups. Mitchell's amendment brought funding up to the spending targets set earlier by Congress in the first Budget Resolution. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Over Administration objections, the House made significant improvements in the nation's housing programs when it passed the 1977 housing authorization bill. Among other provisions, the legislation increased funding available for housing for the elderly and reactivated the public housing construction program. A last-minute motion by Rep. Brown (R-Mich.) to recommit the conference report on the bill to delete these provisions was defeated 157-250 on June 30. For Recommittal - Wrong. Against Recommittal - Right.

corrections: date 1976-06-30 -> 1976-07-01 per Voteview roll 986
aflcio_description: Blocked in their efforts to deregulate natural gas prices, President Ford and his Federal Energy Administration pushed to end price controls on various oil products. They met with partial success as Congress refused to block a proposal to decontrol prices of diesel fuel, home heating oil and other middle distillate fuels. These fuels supply 17 percent of domestic energy needs. The estimated increased cost on home heating bills alone would be over $1 billion. Although Congress has veto power over such decisions, a resolution to block this proposal was tied up in the House Commerce Committee. A motion by Rep. Dingell (D-Mich.) to discharge the resolution from the committee to allow for its floor consideration was defeated by a 194-208 vote on June 30. As a result, the price decontrol proposal went into effect. For Discharge - Right. Against Discharge - Wrong.

Opponents of the unemployment compensation bill sought to eliminate one of the few significant reforms in the legislation. As reported by committee, the bill extended benefit protection to over 8.3 million state and local government workers not previously covered. Rep. Ketchum (R-Calif.) offered an amendment to strike this provision. It was rejected 186-212 on July 20. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

House-passed legislation to improve the federal-state system of unemployment compensation benefits fell far short of overall reforms long sought by the AFL-CIO. A key fight on the bill, strongly opposed by business interests, came on an amendment by Rep. Corman (D-Calif.) providing for a uniform federal standard to upgrade the inadequate maximum benefits paid by most states. The labor-backed amendment would have set the benefits at 50 percent of a person's average weekly wage up to a maximum equal to two-thirds of the statewide average weekly wage. The House rejected the amendment by a 113-281 vote on July 20. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Despite the earlier setback, Congress resurrected and passed a scaled-down version of the vetoed public works measure. The $3.9 billion bill would create over 300,000 jobs. Like the previously vetoed bill, the measure included over $1 billion in aid to financially-strapped cities and states. Again President Ford vetoed the bill. This time, however, Congress rebuffed him. Following the Senate's lead, the House voted 310-96 on July 22 to override the veto. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Each year hundreds of miners lose their lives because of lax enforcement of mine safety laws primarily because the Interior Dept. which enforces these laws is also responsible for maximizing mine production. To end this conflict of interest, the AFL-CIO has long proposed the transfer of job safety functions to the Labor Dept. so that all job safety programs might be under one jurisdiction. Legislation to effect this change was passed by the House despite Administration opposition. Rep. Quie (R-Minn.) offered an Administration-backed substitute bill to prevent this transfer. His proposal was rejected by the House on July 27 by a 119-263 vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: date taken from Voteview roll 1079: the card gives Aug. 9 for the bill's passage and no date for the amendment itself
aflcio_description: In 1972 only 55 percent of the electorate voted in the presidential elections. Two years later only 40 percent of eligible voters cast ballots in congressional elections. Millions of American voters fail to go to the polls each year because of state and local registration laws that actually discourage registration to vote. To curb this decline in voter participation, the AFL-CIO endorsed a bill establishing a national postcard voter registration system which the House approved Aug. 9. During debate on the bill, the House defeated 172-199 an amendment by Rep. Frenzel (R-Minn.) to disallow implementation of the postcard system in 1976 elections and thus discourage Senate action this year. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: date 1977-03-04 -> 1977-03-03 per Voteview roll 35
aflcio_description: Reacting to the need to provide more funds for economic recovery, the House, as part of its third budget resolution revising federal spending for fiscal year 1977, increased President Carter's proposed spending for jobs and local assistance. The extra monies were targeted to such programs as public works, public service jobs and youth employment. The conference report which added $3.4 billion for these economic stimulus programs was approved by a 226-173 vote on Mar. 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

In violation of a United Nations embargo against importing commodities from the racist Rhodesian government, the United States has been importing chromium ore since 1971. That year Sen. Harry Byrd (Ind-Va.) won Senate approval of a proviso prohibiting U.S. adherence to the boycott when it involved strategic materials such as chrome. In 1977, with the strong support of the Carter Administration, Congress approved legislation repealing the Byrd amendment. The House passed its version of the bill by a 250-146 vote on Mar. 14. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

House conservatives backed by some moderate Democrats helped defeat passage of labor-backed situs picketing. The legislation, a goal of organized labor for over a quarter of a century, would have reinstated equal rights for building trades workers to picket an entire job site - a right which industrial workers now have. By a 205-217 vote the House rejected the bill on March 23. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Legislation to outlaw abusive tactics by bill collection agencies was passed by Congress in 1977 and signed into law by President Carter. The legislation curbed harassment of consumers at their workplace and disallowed such practices as late night phone calls and false representation. The House passed the consumer protection legislation by a narrow 199-198 vote on Apr. 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The AFL-CIO endorsed legislation vetoed twice by President Ford providing for federal minimum standards for state strip mining control laws. This environmental bill was signed into law by President Carter in 1977. During House consideration, Rep. Robert Bauman (R-Md.) attempted to have the bill killed by recommitting it to committee. His effort failed by an 83-228 vote on Apr. 29. For recommittal - Wrong. Against - Right.

In 1977 Congress completed action on legislation extending community development funding assistance to financially depressed cities and locales. During debate on the legislation an effort was made to delete a labor-backed spending formula giving priority to those urban areas most in need. The amendment offered by Rep. Mark Hannaford (D-Calif.) was defeated 149-261 on May 10. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Congress approved legislation to extend and expand the program of counter-cyclical funds to help cities and states maintain public services and thus avoid massive layoff of public workers during periods of high unemployment. During House debate the AFL-CIO opposed an amendment by Rep. Les Aspin (D-Wis.) to rewrite the allocation formula so that a smaller share of the funds would have gone to areas with the highest unemployment. This amendment was beaten 127-216 on May 13. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

In debate on the Hatch Act Reform bill, Rep. John Ashbrook (R-Ohio) succeeded in securing House approval of an amendment to disallow unions from using funds for such legal political activities as non-partisan voter registration drives and get-out-the-vote efforts. Later, however, the House approved by a 266-139 vote on June 7 an amendment by Rep. Bill Clay (D-Mo.) effectively nullifying the anti-union Ashbrook amendment. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Federal funding of water resource projects has contributed significantly to the economic development of the nation in such areas as inland water transportation, energy power generation, flood control, water storage and irrigation. These projects have also provided thousands of job opportunities for American workers. In early 1977, the Carter Administration announced its intention to terminate funding for a number of these projects. However, the House on June 14, during debate on a public works appropriations bill rejected 194-218 an Administration supported amendment by Rep. Silvio Conte (R-Mass.) and Butler Derrick (D-S.C.) to kill 16 water projects and cut back one other. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Every year since passage of the landmark job safety law, conservatives have attempted to weaken the Occupational Safety & Health Act. In 1977 Rep. Steven Symms (R-Idaho) tried to slash OSHA funding by $6.3 million for fiscal 1978. The House rejected this effort by a 162-231 vote on June 16. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

During House consideration of 1978 Labor-HEW appropriations, Rep. Bob Michel (R-Ill.) attempted to slash $563.5 million in federal funds for 11 health, education and elderly programs. Opposed by labor, his amendment was beaten 72-334 on June 16. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Legislation to improve federal mine safety laws by consolidating and improving mine safety programs and transferring enforcement functions from the Interior Dept. to the Labor Dept. was signed into law by President Carter in 1977. During House debate on this bill Rep. Ronald Sarasin (R-Mass.) introduced a weaker substitute bill which would have maintained separate laws for hard rock and coal miners. The House rejected the Sarasin substitute by a 151-188 vote on July 15. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Striking workers and their families are entitled to food stamps as long as they comply with the stringent eligibility requirements under the program. During House consideration of a 1977 farm bill which included a four-year extension of the food stamp program, Rep. Richard Kelly (R-Fla.) offered an amendment to deny food stamps to strikers and their families. The House rejected the Kelly amendment by a 170-249 vote on July 27. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

President Carter's national energy program included recommendations to encourage energy conservation by authorizing funds for school, hospital and public building insulation programs. During House debate on the legislation Rep. William Ford (D-Mich.) offered an amendment to extend the wage protections of the Davis-Bacon Act to workers installing insulation. His amendment mandated the payment of the prevailing wage paid for similar work in their areas. By a 265-161 vote on Aug. 2 the House approved the Ford amendment. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Since the 1955 merger convention the AFL-CIO has fought efforts by the energy industry to deregulate federal price controls on natural gas. Deregulation would cost consumers billions of dollars and have a catastrophic effect on the economy. During House consideration of a national energy policy bill, Rep. Clarence Brown (R-Ohio) offered the industry's deregulation amendment which would cost consumers an estimated $71 billion by 1985. The House rejected Brown's amendment by a 199-227 vote on Aug. 3. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

President Carter had recommended increased taxes on domestically produced oil in order to encourage conservation through higher prices. The AFL-CIO strongly opposed this rationing through higher taxes. During debate on House legislation which included the so-called crude oil equalization tax, Rep. James Jones (D-Okla.) tried to return a portion of these tax revenues to the oil industry rather than rebating all of the tax revenues to consumers. The AFL-CIO strongly opposed this amendment which was defeated by a 198-223 vote on Aug. 4. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: tally 210-211 -> 209-211 per Voteview roll 512
aflcio_description: The House rejected a move to establish a subminimum wage rate for non-student workers aged 18 or younger. An amendment offered by Rep. Robert Cornell (D-Wis.) would have allowed employers to pay these workers 85 percent of the minimum wage for the first six months. The AFL-CIO opposed the amendment on the basis that it would not relieve high teenage unemployment and would cause displacement of older workers by younger workers who could be paid less. The House rejected the amendment by a narrow 210-211 vote on Sept. 15. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Conservatives were defeated in an attempt to sidetrack the Labor Law Reform bill and substitute for it an anti-union, employer-backed measure. By a 267-152 count on Oct. 4 the House, in a procedural vote, in effect upheld the rule which only allowed for debate on amendments germane to the substance of the Labor Law Reform legislation. Thus consideration of the anti-worker bill was blocked. For the rule - Right. Against - Wrong.

In 1977 the House approved labor law reform legislation designed to better protect a worker's right to seek union representation. Endorsed by President Carter, the bill expedites the administration and procedures of the National Labor Relations Act while also strengthening penalties against labor law violators. The package of reforms contained in the legislation represents the most important revision in labor law since passage of the 1935 Wagner Act. Overcoming the concerted opposition of business and right-wing groups the House on Oct. 6 approved its version of the legislation by a 257-163 vote. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

To help rebuild the American Merchant Marine, protect the maritime environment and better assure the security of a portion of oil imports, the AFL-CIO backed legislation mandating that a percentage of U.S. oil be carried in American ships. With only 3 percent of oil imports now carried in American vessels, the bill would have boosted that percentage to 9.5 percent by 1981. The legislation would have created an estimated 20,000 maritime related jobs. The House, however, defeated the bill by a 165-257 vote on Oct. 19. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

To help meet the nation's energy demands the AFL-CIO has supported development of all energy resources to best determine their feasibility as future energy sources. As part of its energy program the Carter Administration proposed, however, that development of the Clinch River nuclear breeder reactor demonstration project be discontinued. During debate on Oct. 19 on a supplemental appropriations bill the House approved 252-165 an amendment by Rep. Tom Bevil (D-Ala.) restoring $80 million in funding for the Clinch River project. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: tally 236-187 -> 236-185 per Voteview roll 622
aflcio_description: President Carter on Nov. 1 signed into law labor-backed minimum wage legislation. The final bill increased the minimum wage rate in four steps from the current $2.30 to $3.35 by 1981. The bill also made other significant improvements in the fair wage law. Despite strong opposition from business groups, the House on Oct. 20, approved the conference report on the bill by a 236-187 vote. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

In 1977 the Congress approved legislation to stabilize the financing of the social security system. During House consideration of the bill, Rep. William Ketchum (R-Calif.) offered a crippling amendment phasing out the present limitation on the outside earnings of a social security recipient thus increasing the number of eligible beneficiaries. An increase in employee payroll taxes would finance this provision. His amendment primarily benefits higher income beneficiaries working full time at the expense of higher taxes on low and middle income wage earners. The House approved the amendment by a 268-149 vote on Oct. 27. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

With hundreds of thousands of U.S. jobs disappearing annually as a result of unregulated imports and unfair foreign trade competition, the AFL-CIO renewed labor's support for American preference provisions requiring that all taxpayer-financed federal programs utilize goods and services produced in the United States where available. During debate on legislation to revise the existing law governing development of resources in the outer continental shelf, Rep. John Murphy (D-N.Y.) offered a "buy and build American" requirement mandating the use of American workers and domestically manufactured rigs, platforms and other materials to be used in off-shore production of oil and gas. Ignoring an unemployment rate in excess of 6 percent and the stimulative economic effect of this requirement, the House by a 201-208 vote on Feb. 2 rejected the Murphy amendment. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

In 1978 the AFL-CIO renewed its decade-long fight to win establishment of an Office of Consumer Representation to give consumers an effective voice in the often complex federal policy-making process. The consumer office would also perform a number of other services, consolidating some 26 consumer functions of various government agencies into one centralized consumer agency. Despite the strong support of President Carter and a broad coalition of labor, consumer, farm, and other groups, the House by a 189-227 vote on Feb. 8 killed the consumer agency legislation. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: date 1978-02-23 -> 1978-02-24 per Voteview roll 770
aflcio_description: This taxpayer financed government agency insures private investment abroad against losses from political and other risks. The AFL-CIO has opposed continuation of OPIC because it encourages U.S. firms to invest in other countries, draining this country of much needed investment revenue and resulting in the loss of U.S. jobs and production capabilities. In late February, the House considered a one-year extension of OPIC. Despite a trade deficit approaching $30 billion and unemployment due to imports on the rise, the House approved the extension by a 191-165 margin on Feb. 23. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

In the 95th Congress the AFL-CIO backed legislation introduced by the late Sen. Hubert H. Humphrey and Rep. Augustus F. Hawkins (D-Calif.) designed to make full employment the nation's top economic priority. Full employment would be accomplished primarily through private sector jobs brought about by coordinating fiscal, monetary and employment policies of the federal government to promote healthy, economic growth. The bill set an unemployment rate target of a modest 4 percent to be accomplished by 1983. During consideration of the full employment bill, House Republicans tried to cripple it with weakening amendments. The most serious was an attempt by Rep. James Jeffords (R-Vt.) to gut the bill by equating a lowering of the inflation rate to 3 percent with the 4 percent unemployment goal in the bill. The amendment was rejected 198-223 on Mar. 9. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: tally 259-152 -> 257-152 per Voteview roll 841
aflcio_description: On Mar. 16 the House approved the Humphrey-Hawkins full employment bill 259-152. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Despite standardization of the 40-hour workweek for most private and public employees, some 11,500 firefighters employed by the federal government work a 72-hour week. Although they are on the job 33 percent more hours each week than municipal firefighters, they receive less than 25 percent in additional pay. The AFL-CIO supported legislation sponsored by Reps. Herbert E. Harris (D-Va.) and Patricia Schroeder (D-Colo.) to reduce the workweek to 56 hours and provide overtime pay for work in excess of 54 hours. The House passed this bill 241-129 on Apr. 12, but President Carter later vetoed the measure. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The existing law that regulates congressional lobbying is so riddled with loopholes that the public and Congress are unable to determine how special interest groups work for or against legislation. A major flaw is that groups such as the National Right to Work committee, the National Association of Manufacturers, and other organizations that stimulate so-called grass roots lobbying through mailings to Congress fail to report such activities. During House debate on labor-backed lobbying reform legislation, the AFL-CIO supported an amendment by Rep. Walter Flowers (D-Ala.) to require that registered lobbying organizations fully disclose mass mailing efforts and similar solicitations. The House approved this amendment 245-161 on Apr. 19. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

During debate on the first budget resolution - the initial step in the congressional budget process determining overall federal spending targets - House fiscal conservatives sought wholesale, arbitrary cuts in federal spending. Such was the thrust of an amendment by Rep. Joseph Fisher (D-Va.) to cut the federal budget across the board by 2 percent. Because more than half of the federal budget consists of mandatory, uncontrollable spending for programs like social security, revenue sharing and interest on the public debt, this cut would have to be taken in its entirety from so-called discretionary programs - education, employment, job training, public works, health and defense. Thus $10 billion would have to be cut from these programs. The AFL-CIO strongly opposed the Fisher amendment which was beaten 195-203 on May 9. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Rep. John Ashbrook (R-Ohio) offered an amendment to the first budget resolution to slash spending for the Dept. of Health, Education & Welfare by $3.1 billion. This cut would have drastically reduced spending for education, health, and programs for the elderly. The Ashbrook amendment was defeated 192-205 on May 10. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Organized labor has long been in the forefront of federal, state, and local efforts to provide for free public education for all. For that reason the AFL-CIO strongly opposed in 1978 proposals allowing for a tuition tax credit for families who choose to send their children to private schools. Tuition tax credits would benefit mostly higher income persons and cost the federal treasury several billion dollars in revenue. This revenue loss would eventually be taken out of the total education budget, thus seriously impairing federal aid to the nation's public school system. During debate on legislation to provide tuition tax credits for college education expenses, Rep. Charles Vanik (D-Ohio) offered an amendment to permit tax credits for private elementary and secondary education costs. The estimated revenue loss from the Vanik amendment would be $895 million by 1981. Despite labor's opposition, the Vanik proposal won House approval 209-194 on June 1. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: tally 184-216 -> 183-216 per Voteview roll 1091
aflcio_description: Each year right-wing conservatives in Congress attempt to destroy the landmark 1970 Occupational Safety & Health Act (OSHA), the nation's major industrial safety law. The House ringleader of this anti-worker campaign is Rep. Steven Symms (R-Ida.). In 1978 Symms tried to slash $28.4 million in job safety funding from a labor-HEW appropriations bill. This would have seriously impaired effective enforcement of the law. Although the Symms amendment was initially approved, the House on a second vote on June 13 rejected it by a 184-216 vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

The 1931 Davis-Bacon Act requires the payment of prevailing wages on federally-financed projects to assure that construction workers are paid a fair and equitable wage rate. During House consideration of a housing authorization bill, anti-labor conservatives led by Rep. Thomas M. Hagedorn (R-Minn.) sought to weaken the Davis-Bacon Act provisions relating to this federal program. His amendment proposed that the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirement be waived on housing rehabilitation projects built by neighborhood-based, non-profit organizations. Opponents argued that such a waiver would result in lower pay for black and other minority construction workers. By a 173-218 vote on June 28, the House rejected the Hagedorn amendment. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Federal election financing now is provided only for presidential candidates. The AFL-CIO supports legislation to extend public financing to congressional elections as well. An effort to allow for consideration of a public financing amendment was made during House deliberations on a bill authorizing funds for the Federal Election Commission, but was defeated on a procedural vote sustaining the limited rule by a 213-196 vote on July 19. For sustaining rule - Wrong. Against sustaining rule - Right.

A major weapon against high unemployment is public service jobs funded under the Comprehensive Employment & Training Act (CETA). During House debate on legislation authorizing refunding for CETA, the bill was substantially crippled. A major setback came when the House approved a provision by Rep. David Obey (D-Wis.) to slash the amount of pay a CETA worker could earn on a public service job and to cut back the average CETA wages paid by local jurisdictions. This amendment would effectively remove from the program the ability of most high-wage urban areas to employ CETA workers on entry-level jobs. Despite AFL-CIO opposition, the House approved the Obey amendment by a 230-175 vote on Aug. 9. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

A second assault on the CETA program came against the so-called countercyclical public service jobs for unemployed skilled and semi-skilled workers. Rep. James Jeffords (R-Vt.) offered an amendment to cut this program by a minimum of 100,000 jobs. Again, despite AFL-CIO opposition, the House approved the amendment by a 221-181 vote on Aug. 9. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

After rejecting most of the tax reforms proposed by the Carter Administration and supported by the AFL-CIO, the House Ways & Means Committee adopted a tax cut bill heavily weighted toward upper income taxpayers. The bill also would roll back previous progress in closing capital gains loopholes. In an attempt to repair the damage, a liberal coalition attempted two key modifications in the bill during House floor deliberations. The first proposal was an amendment by Rep. Richard Gephardt (D-Mo.) designed to provide some relief from rising social security taxes by allowing a 5 percent income tax credit for social security taxes paid. However, the proposed rule under which the House was to consider the bill precluded a vote on the Gephardt amendment. An effort by the AFL-CIO and other groups to amend the rule and allow debate on the Gephardt proposal failed 284-130 on Aug. 10. For sustaining rule - Wrong. Against sustaining rule - Right.

A second effort came on an amendment by Reps. James Corman (D-Calif.) and Joseph Fisher (D-Va.) to tilt the overall tax benefits more toward low and middle income-wage earners, limit tax cuts for the rich and reduce capital gains relief. The House rejected the Corman-Fisher amendment on Aug. 10, 193-225. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The Inter-American Development Bank and the International Development Association are two principal foreign aid lending institutions that provide long-term economic improvement loans to less-developed nations and finance various large-scale projects helping low-income workers in these countries. During House debate on foreign aid appropriations legislation, Rep. Clarence Long (D-Md.) sought to cut funds for these two banks by an additional 30 percent on top of the 17 percent already cut from President Carter's budget recommendation. To head off this drastic cut, Rep. David Obey (D-Wis.) offered a substitute amendment for a 2 percent reduction. The House approved the substitute 241-153 on Aug. 14. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

In 1972 Congress overwhelmingly approved a constitutional amendment prohibiting discrimination based on sex. Such an amendment requires ratification by three-fourths - 38 - of the states. With 35 states having approved ERA and a March 1979 ratification deadline approaching, the AFL-CIO threw its support behind House legislation to extend the deadline for an additional seven years. The legislation was vociferously opposed by right-wing conservatives. The extension bill reported by the House Judiciary Committee allowed an additional 39 months for state approval. The key vote came on an amendment by Rep. Thomas F. Railsback (R-Ill.) allowing states to rescind their previous approval of ERA.
